rungs.stem: Jesus pushes a boat out from the shore of the Sea of Galilee, sits down in it while the crowd stands on the beach, and opens a parable with a single farmer image. What is the farmer doing?
choices: Going out to sow seed
Threshing wheat on a stone floor
Pruning back an old grapevine
Digging a well beside his field
rungs.context: Matthew 13:3 KJV: 'Behold, a sower went forth to sow.' The parable of the Sower opens Matthew 13 -- a chapter-long teaching Jesus delivers seated in a boat, using seven parables in a row. Source: KJV Matthew 13.

rungs.stem: In the parable of the Sower, some seed falls on the beaten footpath running alongside the field. Jesus names what happens to that seed almost at once.
choices: The birds come and eat it up
The rain washes it into the ditch
The oxen tread it into the dust
The wind blows it back into the sack
rungs.answer: The birds come and eat it up
rungs.context: Matthew 13:4 KJV: 'And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up.' The 'way side' is the packed footpath at the edge of a Galilean field where seed could not sink in. Source: KJV Matthew 13.

rungs.stem: In the parable of the Sower, seed falls on stony ground where there is only a thin layer of soil over the rock. Jesus says it springs up quickly -- and then something goes wrong.
choices: It withers in the sun because it has no root
It is trampled flat by the shepherd's flock
The stones grow warm and scorch the young shoot
The seed cracks apart before it can send up a stalk
rungs.answer: It withers in the sun because it has no root
rungs.context: Matthew 13:5-6 KJV: '...forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.' Source: KJV Matthew 13.

rungs.stem: In the parable of the Sower, the seed that falls on GOOD ground finally bears fruit. Jesus gives three specific numbers for how much it yields, listed in one order in Matthew and the reverse order in Mark. In Matthew 13:8 the numbers are given in this order:
choices: Hundredfold, sixtyfold, thirtyfold
Thirtyfold, sixtyfold, hundredfold
Sevenfold, seventyfold, seven hundredfold
Tenfold, fiftyfold, hundredfold
rungs.context: Matthew 13:8 KJV: 'But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.' Mark 4:8 reverses the order to ascending -- thirty, sixty, hundred. Source: KJV Matthew 13, Mark 4.

rungs.stem: Most of Jesus's parables are left standing without explanation, but the Sower is one of the very few he DECODES afterward for his disciples. In Matthew 13:22 he names one thing that acts like the thorns and chokes the seed of the word.
choices: The care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches
The false teaching of the elders and the scribes
The pride of learning and the boast of knowledge
The hunger and the thirst and the labour of the field
rungs.answer: The care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches
rungs.context: Matthew 13:22 KJV: 'He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful.' The Sower is one of the very few parables Jesus explains rung by rung. Source: KJV Matthew 13.

rungs.stem: In the same chapter as the Sower, Jesus tells a short parable comparing the kingdom of heaven to a single tiny seed that grows into a bush so large that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches. Which seed does he name?
choices: A grain of mustard seed
A grain of wheat
A grain of barley
A cedar cone from Lebanon
rungs.context: Matthew 13:31-32 KJV: 'The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof.' Source: KJV Matthew 13.

rungs.stem: The 'grain of mustard seed' in Matthew 13 is not a piece of rhetoric with no real plant behind it -- botanists identify it as the black mustard of Galilee, Brassica nigra, whose seed measures only about one to two millimetres across. In good Galilean soil, how tall can that same plant grow in a single season?
choices: Eight to ten feet
About knee-high
As tall as a cedar of Lebanon
Roughly the height of a fig tree at maturity
rungs.context: Black mustard (Brassica nigra) really does grow eight to ten feet tall in the fertile soil of the Levant in a single growing season, forming a woody bush -- large enough for small birds to perch and shelter in. It is botanically an herbaceous annual, not a true tree, so Jesus's 'becometh a tree' is rhetorical scale, but the plant is genuinely dramatic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustard_seed ; biologyinsights.com/how-big-is-a-mustard-seed-tree.

rungs.stem: Matthew, Mark, and Luke all record the same seed-parables, but ONE seed parable is found only in Mark and nowhere else. In it a farmer scatters seed and then 'sleepeth, and riseth night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how' (Mark 4:26-27). What is that Mark-only parable called?
choices: The seed growing secretly
The wheat and the tares
The barren fig tree
The vineyard labourers
rungs.context: Mark 4:26-29 is the only parable unique to Mark's gospel. Its picture of the stages of growth -- 'first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear' -- shows a farmer who cannot force the growth, only wait and reap. Source: KJV Mark 4 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable_of_the_Growing_Seed.
